governing_proposition: Arkansas' greatest productive asset is not its land, corporations, government, natural resources, or financial capital. It is the capability of its people.
demand_principle: Demand informs opportunity. It does not determine a life.
purpose_lock: The purpose of public investment in human capability is not to manufacture workers for Arkansas' economy. It is to give Arkansans greater power to build lives, families, businesses, communities and futures of their own choosing.

sidebar_dignity.title: A person is not an economic input
sidebar_dignity.text: Constitutional Capitalism values human capital, but it does not measure human worth by economic productivity. A child, a disabled Arkansan, a retired person, a caregiver, someone between jobs, someone pursuing art, someone caring for a dying parent — their human dignity doesn't rise or fall with GDP contribution. That's where the Constitutional part constrains the Capitalism part.

rrab.plain: Give people reasons to build lives here.
Make Arkansas a place people who left can realistically come home to.
Welcome people who bring skills, ideas, investment, families and energy.
Residence without connection is incomplete. Belonging comes from community, relationships, institutions, participation, ownership, service, and voice.

sections.heading: Two children, one Arkansas
prose: Meet Jordan and Casey — ILLUSTRATION, not data. Born the same day in Arkansas.

Jordan grows up where schools are strong, broadband works, healthcare is reachable, transportation exists, mentors appear, extracurriculars happen, higher education is nearby, employers and internships exist, and family finances are more stable.
Casey is every bit as capable. Opportunities around them are thinner. This is not a tragedy caricature — it is a different opportunity environment.
Talent is distributed far more broadly than opportunity.
At age five their capabilities may be difficult to distinguish. At 25 their economic choices can look radically different.
Did Arkansas somehow have less human potential in one child? No. Arkansas developed different amounts of it.

sections.heading: Stop calling people “workforce”
prose: Businesses need workers. Governments track labor supply. Economic developers track workforce availability. The term is useful — and incomplete.

A person isn't simply an input into somebody else's production function. A human being can become a worker, entrepreneur, researcher, parent, teacher, artist, farmer, engineer, caregiver, craftsperson, investor, community leader, inventor, public servant, and owner.
Constitutional Capitalism begins with human capability, not merely labor supply.

sections.heading: What is human capital?
prose: Human capital includes accumulated knowledge, skills, experience, health, judgment, relationships, adaptability, creativity, and productive capability.
Unlike a machine, the human being owns a life.
We invest in people for their flourishing and agency — not merely because somebody needs an employee.

sections.heading: The Capability Continuum
prose: Life is continuous development: early childhood → K–12 → career/technical → college/university → apprenticeship → work → entrepreneurship → continuous learning → service/leadership → mentorship.

Do not draw a single straight ladder. Draw interconnected pathways. People move sideways, backward, forward. Change careers. Return to education. Start businesses. Leave employment. Re-enter. Care for family. Serve. Retire and mentor.
That's closer to real life.

sections.heading: Multiple pathways, equal dignity
prose: Public policy often accidentally creates a hierarchy: college = success; everything else = alternative. Reject that.

A four-year degree can create enormous value. So can technical education, skilled trades, apprenticeships, certifications, military experience, entrepreneurship, agriculture, care work, and other pathways.
Which pathway expands this person's capability and realistic opportunity?
Pathways should remain permeable. A welder should be able to become an engineer. A soldier a teacher. A teacher an entrepreneur. An entrepreneur should be able to return to university.
No educational choice at 18 should become a caste assignment.

sections.heading: Demand Map — without letting the economy choose lives
prose: Arkansas should understand what skills employers seek, where shortages may exist, where industries are growing, what occupations are changing, and where geographic mismatches exist. That's useful information.
Demand informs opportunity. It does not determine a life.
If Arkansas needs 3,000 workers in a field, government doesn't get to decide that 3,000 particular teenagers belong in that field.
Give people information. Build pathways. Let human choice remain central.

sections.heading: A “shortage” isn't always a shortage of people
prose: An employer says: We can't find workers.

Possible explanation: not enough trained people. Also possibly: wages, schedule, location, childcare, transportation, housing, working conditions, credential requirements, or competition from better opportunities.
A labor shortage can sometimes be a signal about the job rather than the worker.
That prevents the state from automatically subsidizing employer labor problems.

sections.heading: Health is productive capacity — and dignity is not GDP
prose: A person who cannot obtain needed healthcare may miss work, leave employment, reduce hours, be unable to train, care for another family member, or experience diminished quality of life.
Health affects human flourishing and productive capability.
Do not reduce healthcare to economic productivity. A retired Arkansan has value even if they never generate another dollar of GDP. Human dignity isn't conditional on economic output.

sections.heading: Time is capability
prose: Connect to Chapter 2. Someone may technically have access to a course — but work two jobs, lack childcare, drive long distances, face unpredictable schedules, or lack transportation.
Opportunity that a person cannot realistically use is incomplete opportunity.
Time, transportation, digital access, and care capacity become part of human-capital infrastructure.

sections.heading: The geography of opportunity
prose: Return to Phillips County carefully — contrast, do not demean.

Can a talented child in every Arkansas county realistically reach advanced coursework, career training, mentors, high-speed internet, healthcare, capital, internships, employers, universities, markets?
Not necessarily physically in every community. Technology and regional systems can connect people.
The objective isn't to duplicate every institution in all 75 counties.
Geography should shape how opportunity is delivered without determining how much opportunity a person deserves.

sections.heading: Community capital
prose: Highly capable people alone don't automatically create a prosperous place. A community also needs relationships and institutions that allow people to coordinate.
The Community Capital Pentagon — five certified dimensions of place capability interacting — teaches: Human capital can leave. Community capital gives human capability somewhere to take root.
That prepares Retain → Return → Attract → Belong.

sections.heading: Why talented people leave
prose: Don't shame them. People leave for education, careers, relationships, culture, housing, higher wages, adventure, specialized services, or simply because they want to.
A free society permits that.
Arkansas' objective isn't to trap people. It is to become a place people have meaningful reasons to choose.

sections.heading: Retain → Return → Attract → Belong
prose: RETAIN: Give people reasons to build lives here.
RETURN: Make Arkansas a place people who left can realistically come home to.
ATTRACT: Welcome people who bring skills, ideas, investment, families and energy.
BELONG: Economic-development plans often miss this. A person can physically reside somewhere and never become connected to it.
Prosperous places aren't merely places people move to. They're places people become invested in.

sections.heading: Residency and public investment
prose: Arkansas invests heavily in people through public institutions. The certified architecture uses bona fide residency — not citizenship — as the relevant frame for resident public-investment benefits where lawful.
A state is a geographic political community. It can have legitimate reasons to distinguish residents from nonresidents in certain programs where law permits.
This cannot become hostility toward newcomers. Constitutional Capitalism wants people to become Arkansans.
Prevent benefit tourism — not talent immigration.

sections.heading: Education as intergenerational capital
prose: A public school expenditure disappears from the annual budget ledger. The capability it creates can last decades.
Classifying every public dollar simply as 'spent' can hide important differences. Some expenditures consume resources now. Others may build capability that produces future value.
The return isn't necessarily government cash — higher capability, earnings, innovation, health, lower fragility, stronger communities, greater civic participation.
Public value is not the same as public cash. COUNTABLE remains $0.

sections.heading: Research → prosperity
prose: Universities create research, technology, companies, patents, process improvements, medical discoveries, agricultural innovation, and intellectual property.

When the public bears meaningful risk or contributes meaningful capital, the public may have a legitimate claim to a proportionate share of resulting economic upside — when legally and contractually structured.
Not all research. Not all intellectual property. Not government seizure. Public claim proportional to public contribution and risk — joining Chapter 3's eight-gate standard.

sections.heading: Worker → owner
prose: Human capability produces income. Prosperity Surplus can create savings. Savings can become investment. Investment can become ownership. Ownership can produce returns.
LEARN → EARN → RETAIN → SAVE → OWN → COMPOUND.
Preserve Stage 4: diversify. Do not put a household's entire economic future into one employer.

sections.heading: Service as capital
prose: People build community capability through military service, teaching, emergency response, mentorship, public service, nonprofit work, civic leadership, caregiving, and other contribution.
Not all value creation appears as corporate profit.
The state and community can recognize legitimate service without turning citizenship into a transactional point system. Principle — not a new program.

sections.heading: AI changes the bargain
prose: Don't predict apocalypse. AI may allow fewer people to produce more output. It may change, create, and eliminate tasks and occupations. Reduce costs. Concentrate returns. Increase productivity. Nobody knows the exact distribution.
A society built entirely around training people for today's jobs is increasingly fragile.
Capability must include adaptability, reasoning, creativity, communication, technical fluency, civic understanding, and continuous learning.

sections.heading: Retraining is not a magic wand
prose: Stage 4 killed that claim. Say so.

A 58-year-old whose occupation disappears cannot necessarily become a software engineer after a six-week course. Some transitions will be difficult. Some regions have too few alternative employers. Some skills won't transfer. Some wages may never fully recover.
Constitutional Capitalism does not answer technological displacement with 'Just retrain.'
It asks about capability, ownership, transition support, market structure, productivity distribution, community resilience, and time.

sections.heading: Who owns the productivity?
prose: Suppose AI allows one company to produce twice as much with half as much labor. Society is more productive. Who receives the gain — consumers, workers, owners, shorter workweeks, government, some combination?
The technology doesn't answer that. Institutions and ownership do.
That connects AI directly to Constitutional Capitalism rather than creating an AI-policy tangent.

sections.heading: Human capability is not centrally planned
prose: Government should help create information, pathways, institutions, access, infrastructure, rules, and legitimate public investment.
It should not assign human beings to economic roles.
A prosperous Arkansas needs people free to surprise us. Someone may create an industry the Demand Map never predicted. That's part of what markets and human freedom are for.

sections.heading: Capability without community
prose: Return to Jordan and Casey. Imagine both become enormously capable. But one concludes: There is nowhere here for me to build the life I want.
Human-capital investment walks out the door. That doesn't mean the investment was wasted — the person still matters.
From Arkansas' economic perspective, it reveals the second half: capable people + capable places.

sections.heading: The capability flywheel
prose: Healthy child → education → skills → opportunity → productive work/enterprise → income → Prosperity Surplus → ownership → community investment → stronger institutions → greater opportunity for the next child.
Escape arrows: poor health, unaffordable housing, weak opportunity, capture, lack of capital, displacement, fragility.
The flywheel isn't automatic. Institutions determine whether it compounds.

sections.heading: Return to the children
prose: Don't make one 'win' and one 'lose.' Give them different lives. Perhaps one becomes a skilled tradesperson and business owner. Another leaves for education, builds a career, and eventually returns — or doesn't. Both are legitimate.

The purpose of public investment in human capability is not to manufacture workers for Arkansas' economy. It is to give Arkansans greater power to build lives, families, businesses, communities and futures of their own choosing.
And when people have reasons to build those lives here, Arkansas becomes stronger too.
Next: the productive systems that must actually function every day for capable people and prosperous households to build lives in Arkansas.
